title: Gone beyond
hookLine: the mantra: gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha, gone, gone beyond (Heart Sutra)
tomorrow: Confucius had a crowd of students. which one loved to learn?

cards: A ferry bumps the dock on the far side, and everyone on deck feels it. Arrived. The Heart Sutra ends on a feeling like that.
After all its talk of emptiness, it gives a mantra, in Sanskrit: gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha. Gone, gone, gone beyond, gone all the way beyond, awakening, so be it.
The sutra calls it the great mantra that calms all suffering. Four steps across the water, and then: awake.

teach.h: A FLOOD, NO BOAT, NO BRIDGE.
teach.b: Beyond what? The Buddha told a story about it. A man comes to a great flood.
This shore is dangerous; the far shore is safe; there's no boat and no bridge.

teach.h: A RAFT OF GRASS AND STICKS.
teach.b: So he gathers grass, sticks and branches, ties them into a raft, and paddles across with his hands and feet.

teach.h: DON'T CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD.
teach.b: On the far side he thinks: this raft was so useful, I'll carry it on my head wherever I go. Is that wise? No, says the Buddha.
Set it down and walk on. I've taught you the dharma like a raft, he says: for crossing over, not for holding on to.
That's the teaching behind gone beyond. In Buddhism, the far shore is awakening, and even the teaching is a raft. You use it fully, and you don't make it one more thing to cling to.
That fits the sutra itself, which says there is no attainment, since there is nothing to attain. Gone beyond.

how: Mahayana Buddhists chant the Heart Sutra's closing mantra, gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha, often in its Sanskrit sound even when the rest is chanted in their own language.

o: left this world behind for good, never to return
crossed all the way over to the far shore
gone ahead of everyone else in a race

games.q: the mantra and the raft: tap the pairs.

s: 'gone beyond' in the mantra just means a danger is over
it's crossing to the far shore of awakening: gone beyond, all the way beyond, awake.
the Buddha compared his own teaching to a raft you set down
for crossing over, not for holding on to.
the Heart Sutra says the mantra should never be spoken aloud
it gives the mantra plainly at the end and calls it the great mantra that calms all suffering.

games.q: a habit got you through a hard year: a strict routine, a playlist, a rule. the year's over. what would the raft story suggest?
o: thank it, and set it down if it's done its work; it was for crossing.
never drop it; whatever helped once must be carried for life.
it was never really useful; the far shore was there all along.
games.why: the raft was truly useful, and once across, you don't carry it on your head.

practice: Say the mantra out loud, once, slowly, a word to a breath: gate, gate, paragate, parasamgate, bodhi, svaha. Then let the room go quiet, and sit on the far side of the sound until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Gone beyond: paragate, from the Heart Sutra's mantra, crossing to the far shore of awakening.

orig.s: गते गते पारगते पारसंगते बोधि स्वाहा
orig.say: GUH-tay GUH-tay PAH-ruh-guh-tay PAH-ruh-sum-guh-tay BOH-dhee SVAH-hah
orig.note: Sanskrit, the Heart Sutra's mantra: gone, gone, gone beyond, gone all the way beyond, awakening, so be it.

carryVoice: One to keep: gone beyond, and the raft set down on the shore. Two weeks, two crossings, see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra, closing (the great mantra that allays all suffering; gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha)
Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the parable of the raft: for crossing over, not for grasping)
